utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thanks. I must remind you that the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing else but the truth still binds you. You are still expected to tell the same truth, as you did take the oath at the beginning. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, good morning.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You testified yesterday that the only legitimate armed force in Croatia in summer of 1991 was the JNA. Do you remember telling us that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And you considered the Croatian armed forces at the time to be illegitimate; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you also consider the Serb armed forces in the Krajina at that time to be illegitimate?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were not armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, you're not denying that in Krajina there were Serb armed forces in the summer of 1991, are you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were none.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you know that on the 1st of April, 1991, the SAO Krajina Executive Board ordered the mobilisation of SAO Krajina Territorial Defence? Did you know about that, or is that something you didn't know about, now or at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that those were territorial forces. I would say that they were people who were opposed and would not accept the ideology of the newly arising Croatian party.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, regardless of --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, regardless of what they were opposed to or what their ideology was, they were called or they were the SAO Krajina Territorial Defence, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let us say that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That was the case. We're not just going to say that. That was the case. After April 1991, that was when the SAO Krajina Executive Board created the Territorial Defence of SAO Krajina and then they were established throughout 1991. That is the case, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. They were provoked and compelled to do that, because the Serb people in Croatia was left out of the constitution as a nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Things will go much more quickly for us if you will focus on my questions and just answer the question rather than giving some kind of speech, okay? And in that last answer you answered the question with the first words. It wasn't necessary to continue. Now my next question is that there were also Serb police units in the summer of 1991, right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where, Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In the Krajina. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come back to this topic a little later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, I just wanted to get an answer. Now that the witness answered "yes, that's right" to the question that that was the case, we are not just going to say that. After April 1991, that was when the SAO Krajina Executive Board created a Territorial Defence of the SAO Krajina and then they were established throughout 1991. The answer was: "Yes, that's right." The question is: Were they then legitimate? That was the original question you had asked. I beg your pardon. Were they illegitimate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That they were legitimate, yes. Yes. Only the then SFRY Presidency established that all the armed forces that were outside any legislation were illegitimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry. I'm sorry. Your answer has got two contradictory statements. You said that they were legitimate, yes. Yes. Only then -- then you say they were illegitimate. I'm not quite sure. Just answer my question: Was the Territorial Defence of the SAO Krajina that was established in April 1991 illegitimate? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is no yes or no answer to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm afraid I am going to have to interrupt you. You are going to have to say yes or no. There is a yes or no answer to that question. It's a very simple and straightforward question. Based on your testimony yesterday that the only legitimate armed forces in 1991 was the JNA, the question then becomes: Were the Territorial Defence of the SAO Krajina in 1991 illegitimate, yes or no? A simple and straightforward question, based on the logic of your own testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It was not illegitimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How can you explain why you consider the Croatian armed forces illegitimate but you don't consider the Serb armed forces illegitimate? Or have I misunderstood you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You haven't misunderstood me. I consider them to be not illegitimate because the Serb people had carried out a referendum with a view to obtaining their right to remaining within the framework of Yugoslavia, just as Croatia decided to secede. And with its only purpose of having people, the Serb people speak their mind about deciding to stay in Yugoslavia and having done that, that very point is by me considered to be the basis for its legitimacy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So now you are changing the standard for legitimacy, you're not saying that only the JNA was a legitimate armed force. You're saying that the JNA was a legitimate and the Serbs, because they agreed with -- because they had a referendum that said they wanted to stay in Yugoslavia, that's what you're saying now. That's the test of legitimacy for you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Essentially you're saying that -- now why is that the case? Is it because the JNA and the Serbs then have the same goals? Is that what you're saying? Is that why the Serb armed forces in Krajina are legitimate?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same goal was to remain within the community of nations in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. That same goal was shared by the JNA and by the Serbs in Croatia, they wanted to stay within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But by the summer of 1991, of course, Croatia and Slovenia had declared their independence, so there really was no more Yugoslavia, was there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a forcible secession. It was not as a result of an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, the Serb TO and police in Krajina, they weren't the result of any agreement, certainly not with Croatia, were they?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My starting point is that every nation, people, has the right to decide about his or her -- his own fate and that includes the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Does that also include the Croat people in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They exercised this right of theirs, but through different methods.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What different methods do you mean?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatia was not in any way forced to join Yugoslavia. In 1943 Slovenia and Croatia entered the framework of Yugoslavia of their own will, based on -- this was at the meeting of Avnoj. At the same time, it was stipulated that one could not leave the union forcibly or unilaterally. The Avnoj had as its starting point the right of self-determination. This right was present there and Croatia voluntarily became part of Yugoslavia. Croatia also became part of Yugoslavia as the result of an agreement, and likewise it could only secede from Yugoslavia based on an agreement, not by force.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So you're saying that even though Croats have a right to self-determination, they can't actually exercise that right unless the Serbs in Yugoslavia agree with them to exercise it. That's what you're saying, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying the following. If one party decides to secede, then this has to be consensually, with the consent of all the other elements of that unit. Croatia did not adhere to the Avnoj decision, except for the part of this decision where it is stipulated that the internal borders should remain valid. However, one had to listen to the will of the people and not go against that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So to go back to my question, you're saying that even though Croats have a self -- right to self-determination, they can't actually exercise that right unless the Serbs in Yugoslavia agree with them and allow them to exercise that right. That's what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not just the Serbs. All the other nations forming Yugoslavia too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So Croatians can't exercise their right to self-determination unless all the other nations, including the Serbs, agree with them and allow them to secede. That's your view of the way things were?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My view at the time was that the right to self-determination had been historically consumed by the Croats. It was present there in 1943 at the Second Congress of Avnoj, Anti-Fascist National Liberation Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me just focus you on the 1990s because that's really what we're focussed on here, okay? And in the 1990s, I understand you to be saying, and I want you to correct me if I'm wrong about this, but you're saying Croatians couldn't exercise their right to self-determination without the agreement of the Serbs and the other nations in Yugoslavia. That's what you're saying. Without agreement from all the nations, Croatians cannot exercise their right to self-determination.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Black, didn't the witness explain you that his opinion is that this right of the Croats had been consumed in 1943? This is what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no idea what that means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: That would mean there was no right anymore. It was consumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Witness, do you understand? So you're saying that after 1943 the Croats no longer had a right to self-determination. They exercised it in 1943 and then they no longer had it. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Despite the fact that self-determination was referred to in the Yugoslav constitution, it no longer existed for the Croats after 1943, that's what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not just for the Croats. For all the peoples that made up Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What do you mean not just for Croats, for all the peoples. Are you saying that the right to self-determination no longer existed for any of the peoples of the former Yugoslavia after 1943, after this agreement that you've talked about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the right enjoyed by the republics as federal units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So in your view, is the right to self-determination, is that something that belongs to republics or to peoples?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The right was primarily enjoyed or belonged to the peoples, but -- and I mean the peoples within federal units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand what you mean by "primarily enjoyed or belonged to the peoples." Did the republics have a right to self-determination?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Avnoj decisions of the time did not contain that. In the preamble to the constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, it was stipulated in general terms that the republics as federal units had as their starting point the right of their peoples to self-determination. This was contained in the preamble to the SFRY constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So to go back to my question, did the republics have a right to self-determination or was that only something that the peoples had?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the Avnoj decision --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, let me interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- stated in no uncertain terms that the peoples ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Don't -- you don't need to go back to the Avnoj decision and more history lessons. Did the republics have a right to self-determination? You talked to me about the people. But earlier, you know, you referred to rights enjoyed by the republics, and I just want to find out if you're telling us that the republics had the right to self-determination.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So earlier when you said you were referring to the right enjoyed by republics as federal units, what were you talking about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was talking about the peoples living in these federal units, about the peoples themselves. In the federal unit of Croatia, under the constitution, there were two constituent nations, Croats and Serbs, and ethnic -- and minorities. In the new constitution of Croatia, the Serbs were thrown out of the constitution as a constituent nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, we had plenty of evidence about this, so I'm not going to ask you to go into that topic anymore. But let me just ask you one final question on this. In practical terms, how do you say that the right to self-determination can be exercised by people in the republics? According to you, how would that work? How do those peoples exercise their right to self-determination?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb people in Croatia as a constituent nation, until the new Croatian constitution was promulgated, did not agree with the idea of seceding from Yugoslavia. As -- if the Croatian people in Croatia, as a constituent nation, thought that they had the right to self-determination and to secede from Yugoslavia, then likewise by the same token the Serb people in Croatia also thought that they had the right to decide to stay within Yugoslavia, as a unit within which the Serb people are able to exercise their right in Croatia. Their rights in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: According to you, let's assume that the Croats in Croatia decided that they wanted to have a separate country. They wanted to exercise their right to self-determination to have an independent country. You would agree that they have the right to make that decision, right? Just talking about rights.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As Croatia was a state of two peoples, it was not possible for just one peoples in this case, the Croats, to decide about the fate of the country. The Serb people were also a constituent nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, sir, that's my question. And I'm just wondering, you know, you say that the Croat people have a right to self-determination. You say you don't dispute that. But practically speaking, how could they exercise that right if they can't make any decisions without the agreement of the Serb people in Croatia? How is it supposed to work, according to you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't even want to listen to the Serb people who wanted to remain in Yugoslavia. With the stroke of a pen, they simply left the Serbs out of the constitution as a constituent nation. And in Bosnia you had three constituent nations. The Serb people in Croatia were deprived of their right to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- a constituent nation and to decide about the fate of the country together with the other constituent nations, the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You haven't answered my question. And that is, practically speaking, according to you, how were the Croats in Croatia supposed to exercise this right to self-determination that you say they had? I just want to know how you think it should have worked, practically speaking.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the Croats as the people. I'm talking about the political establishment of Croatia who wanted to exercise this right without consulting the Serbs. Because they did not acknowledge them as a people, and I mean they did not acknowledge them in the legislation, in the constitution, because Croatia was a state of both the Serb and Croat peoples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. Are you able to answer this question, or are you not able to answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In fact, I'm trying to comprehend what the gentleman is saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, let me --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it seems that he doesn't understand me either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No. Let me tell you what the gentleman is saying. The gentleman is just asking you to tell us how, in your view, the Croatian people in Croatia should have gone about exercising their right to self-determination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have a problem, Mr. Martic? I see Mr. Martic is standing up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. I wanted to hand this note to the guard to give to my counsel, and the guard is refusing. So far I've had no problems of this sort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would request that -- security guard to please pass on the notes for Mr. Martic, if he has any notes to pass on to his counsel. Thank you very much. So the question is just that simple, sir. How, in your view, do you suggest the Croats should have gone about determining their self-determination -- exercising their right to self-determination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am not legislator nor a constitutional expert. But the Croats did what they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you found fault with what they did. You're finding fault with what they did. And the question then is: What was the correct way of doing things? That's the only question that you are being asked. You either are able to answer the question, or you are not able to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, they could have reached an agreement with the Serb people and found a common political platform as to how to overcome the problem. If the Serb people in Croatia also want to exercise their right to self-determination, then the Croatian authorities should reach an agreement with the Serb people as to how this can be gone about. The Serb people had already said that they wanted to remain in Yugoslavia. The Croatian authorities that were in power at the time wanted to secede from Yugoslavia. However, they had to take into account the Serb people who had expressed their will to remain within Yugoslavia. They did not want to leave Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if I've made myself clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't know if that is the answer you get. I don't know whether you're happy with that. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I guess just one final question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, absent an agreement between the Croatian people and the Serb people, you can't think of any other way in which the Croat people might have exercised, legitimately exercised their right to self-determination? Is that what we're to understand?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not sure that what I'm going to say is an objection, but I would like to remind my learned friend from the Prosecution that this witness is a colonel, not an expert in constitutional law.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness was the one who got into this subject matter and that's the only reason I've gone down this road. If he can answer this question, I will try to get past it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not the witness who imposed this topic. It is the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will like -- I would like to say, if you insist --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Just a second. Can you just keep quiet a little bit. Mr. Perovic, isn't the Prosecutor asking the witness about issues to which the witness had testified?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The topic that has been discussed for about 45 minutes now is very technical. All the questions asked so far belong in the area of constitutional law and law in general. This witness has tried to explain what he believes should have been done, but I don't see any sense in continuing this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, the sense will appear maybe if you allow the questions to go on, Mr. Perovic, because this witness testified to the rights of the Serbs to set up SAO Krajina, and he criticised the Croats for wanting to break away from Yugoslavia. You know, if he invites that kind of questioning by making statements about that and doesn't stick to the area of being a colonel, then he must answer. And I don't think these are difficult constitutional questions. These are questions that can be answered by anybody who expresses an opinion on them on the street, as just how he sees things unfolding, you know. It's not a constitutional matter. It is a constitutional matter if we decide about it as a people, as a nation or two nations. But if we are expressing opinions on the street, we just say, tell us what you think, because you've expressed an opinion on it. I think your objection is overruled, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember my question? Maybe I should state it for you one more time. And if you don't know, you know, just tell us that you don't know. Absent an agreement between the Croat people and the Serb people in Croatia, you can't think of any other way in which the Croat people could have legitimately exercised their right to self-determination? Is that a correct and accurate statement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, the most honest thing would have been for the Croatian authorities to have organised the plebescite. However, that didn't happen. It should have been a plebescite for the Serb and the Croat people in Croatia. It was all one-sided. They used their power to secede. And the Serbs were practically forced to organise themselves separately because they saw themselves as being left out, thrown out of the constitution. They were no longer a category in the constitution. They were non-existent.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well I think you may be mixing a couple of ideas there. It's true, isn't it, that Croatia organised a referendum on independence. They did exactly what you just suggested that they should have done.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they did not do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me go back briefly to my question about the legitimacy of armed forces. You finally answered and -- Judge Moloto when he asked you about the Territorial Defence, and you said that you considered the Serb -- the SAO Krajina Territorial Defence legitimate. Did you also consider the SAO Krajina police and police special units legitimate armed forces in 1991, summer?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were legitimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me move on to another topic, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Just two questions, please, before you do. Mr. Peric, you had given evidence that in 1943 Croatia consumed its right for self-determination. You recall that evidence? It's a right of self-determination. What I want to know from you is this: When you say Croatia, are you referring to Croatia, the land, the republic; or Croatia, indicating the people? The Croatian people, as opposed to the Serb people. Which one were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean the Croat people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: So you're not referring to the republic, then, of Croatia? No. So the next question I want you to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: What it is that they did, the Croat people that took place in 1943, why you say that that right was consumed and exercised and could never be re-exercised again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that decision says proceeding from the right of peoples to self-determination, the Croat people voluntarily joined the community of Yugoslavia. So that self-determination, that right to self-determination existed then. They used it to opt for a union. And that was the second time that the Croat people were joining a community and then leaving it. In 1918 was the first time. After the First World War, they joined the union with Serbs. They did the same in 1943. And both times they wanted to renege on it and leave. And now when they joined the European Union five years later, they'll want to leave it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Are you saying, then, that properly speaking neither the Croats or the Serbs should have exercised the right to self-determination again? But by reason of the fact that the Serbs -- sorry, the Croats illegitimately did so, the Serbs of necessity were compelled to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Serbs were not asking to leave Yugoslavia. The Croats did. Serbs wanted to stay within that union. Within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: But are you saying that Serbs would have had the right to leave, if they wanted? But the Croats would not have? That's not what you're saying? Or are you saying both did not have the right to leave, but because one left illegitimately the other was compelled to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. Precisely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, let me take you now to a different subject. You testified yesterday about arms obtained by Croatia and you said that the JNA reported on those activities. Did the JNA also compile reports on the arming of Serbs in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Units on the territory of the Republic of Croatia were all required to submit daily reports. As far as my sector is concerned that I was in charge of, that was the border belt, I know that I received from subordinate commands daily and monthly reports, and by the chain of command I forwarded them to the General Staff. As for other units, I don't know what they reported and what they wrote in their reports and to whom they submitted them, or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So you simply don't know whether the JNA reported on the arming of Serbs in Croatia, is that what you're saying? Because you didn't -- outside of your unit, you didn't know what was reported on?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about my sector, the border belt and the ten organisational units, that is ten border battalions and what I received from them. And I know what I reported to my superior command, that is the Zagreb army district. What others did in the rest of the territory of Croatia in their own areas of responsibility, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So I guess it's fair to say, then, that while you were based in Zagreb, you didn't know what was happening or being reported on in other parts of Croatia such as the Krajina, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you couldn't say that I didn't know anything, because I had the duty service in the operation centre, because -- and that centre received daily reports from units. I also had the opportunity to see for myself what was going on on the ground. But only in my territory, the border belt. I knew the situation there at any moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So you didn't have an opportunity to see the situation on the ground in the Krajina, did you? In Knin, Bankovac, Obrovac, those municipalities of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You testified yesterday you were based in Zagreb during all of 1990 and up until August of 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So during that time you simply don't know whether Serbs were also -- or whether Serbs were being armed in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know only what I could learn from media reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And what did you learn from media reports about the arming of Serbs in Krajina, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean what I learned from media reports?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes. I asked you if you knew whether Serbs were being armed in the Krajina, and you said "I know only what I could learn from media reports." So if you did learn something about -- that from media reports, go ahead and please tell us what you learned.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that I learned bits of information that I could piece together from the reports arriving at the operation centre, and I learned that in Knin Serb policemen refused to wear the emblems of the new Croatian police, including the chequer-board emblem, and they refused to put it on their caps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That was in July 1990, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What I was really asking about was about the arming of Serbs, about Serbs, people being -- obtaining weapons or being given weapons in the Krajina region. Did you learn anything about that from the media, in 1990 or 1991? I'm really focused on the time you were in Zagreb, up until August of 1991.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know anything about any organised arming of the Serb people. I learned about individuals or groups arming themselves. I learned about the organisation of village guards, et cetera, but nothing organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So you didn't hear about how Milan Martic and other people had distributed weapons to Serbs in the Krajina in August of 1990? You didn't learn about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned that from media reports that I don't know how many pieces of weapons were seized from a police station and distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And in that media report, did you -- did you learn then that Milan Martic was the leader of that effort?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we first learned of an armed operation that happened in Petice -- Plitvice in March 1991. And before that, we heard about Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. I will ask you a little bit about Plitvice later, maybe. But what was it that you heard about Milan Martic before Plitvice?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we heard that he was a policeman at a police station in Knin and that he refused to accept those new Croatian insignia and that he had a group of like-minded policemen supporting him in this refusal and that he was the leader of that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And did you -- was he connected at all in the media reports that you heard with the incident that you talked about where weapons were seized from a police station and distributed? Do you remember if he was connected to that event?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember. I know there was a large crowd protesting outside the police station, trying to find out who removed the weapons from the police station. My memory is no longer that good; I suppose I'm getting on. I can't remember the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So you don't remember any other details, other than that weapons were seized from a police station and distributed, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying I don't remember. Time takes its toll. I know there was a large crowd of people around that police station and I think it was an attempt by the Croatian Ministry of the Interior to intervene and send helicopters -- helicopters to Knin, and I think that was prevented by the units of the JNA air force who were on duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The effect that is sort of getting lost in here, which I think I would like to get an answer to. The question is: Do you remember if Mr. Milan Martic was connected with the seizure of weapons from the police station in Knin and their distribution to the people? I think you should be able to answer that one very clearly by either a yes or no. Yes, I remember. No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I remember there was a commotion and a crowd around that station who ordered the weapons to be seized. I don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. I'm not asking you about a crowd. I'm asking you about Mr. Milan Martic. Do you remember if Mr. Milan Martic was connected with the seizure of weapons from the police station in Knin and their distribution to the people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't remember him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. That's it. That's it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, again moving on to a new topic now. You testified yesterday that from the end of August 1991 and through September, JNA facilities in Croatia were blockaded and JNA convoys were attacked. Do you remember telling us about those things?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, do we need to clear something up on the record? Or should I proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, I'm going to ask you about some things that happened before this time-period of August/September 1991. I guess first a general question about how things operated before. Before 1990, in Yugoslavia, before 1990, Territorial Defence units may have been under JNA command for -- if they were combat operations, but it was actually the republics that trained and equipped the Territorial Defence units. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And it was the republics that were responsible for buying the TO uniforms, for the weapons and other equipment. That was the responsibility of the republics?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly how that was arranged at the federal level, whether some of the funds came from the federal budget or not, or it was financed exclusively by the republics, but I doubt it was exclusively the republics. In any case, I'm not qualified to answer that question, because I was not part of the overall command and control system to be able to tell you what happened on the level of republics, in terms of planning and funding. That goes beyond my professional knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If that goes beyond your knowledge, I won't ask you any more questions about that specific issue. In May 19 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Can I just get clarity on a point. I understand your point and I would like you just to say you don't know if you don't know. But you answered at the administrative level who decides where the money comes from, where the funding comes from. My question would be: Is it correct, then, that the actual buying of the uniforms and equipment on the ground, irrespective of where the funds came from, was done by the republics? Or do you not know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you mean TO units, Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm saying I don't know for certain whether it was solely the republics that were required to finance that on their own or maybe the federal budget participated to some extent, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what I'm trying to move away from. I'm moving away from the finance. I'm talking about the actual purchase on the ground. The finance might have come from the federal government. It might have come from the republic. It might have come from both. Who went and placed the order for equipment and for the uniform? Was it the republics? Or was it the federal government? In other words, did the federal government buy these things and deliver them to the republics, or did the federal government provide the money and the republics bought them? If you do know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as I know, the exclusive right to place orders and purchase equipment belonged to the federal level, the Federal Secretariat for National Defence. Republics individually were not entitled to purchase weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's quite all right, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, when I first asked you this question, I asked you if it was the republics that trained and equipped the Territorial Defence units. And you said "correct." And now I'm confused. It was the republics that were responsible for equipping the Territorial Defence units, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we're talking at cross-purposes here. The republics were the federal units doing all the planning based on a programme produced by the defence ministry and the Federal Secretariat for All People's Defence. They trained their units based on their programmes and they supplied throughout the former Yugoslavia. There was a single training programme, a single equipment procurement programme. But the sole right rested squarely with the federal organs, in terms of purchasing and obtaining equipment. This right was not granted to the republics to do whatever they like in terms of purchasing and importing weapons. This was definitely done at the federal level, as far as the importing or purchasing of any arms equipment, ordinance went. That at least is my understanding of the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So I'm not really -- I'm not really concerned about the general programme. But isn't it the case that the republics actually paid for weapons and uniforms and equipment for the Territorial Defence. That was the responsibility of the republics, according to the scheme, the federal scheme, but it was the republics that paid that money and placed the orders and all of those things. Am I correct about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the financing aspect is concerned, that's all I'm talking about, it's a situation that I am unfamiliar with. As far as the actual placing of orders was concerned, I know that it was down to the federal bodies to do that. As for the financing aspect, whether the money came from the coffers of the republics or the federal ones is, quite frankly, not something that I was interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And I think you've said that you simply don't know where the financing came from, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't into that sort of thing at the time at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In May of 1990, the JNA ordered that TO weapons and the republics be taken over by the JNA and stored in JNA warehouses. You remember that, don't you, in May of 1990?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may be a slip on your part, but you say that the TO should take over weapons from the JNA and place weapons in JNA warehouses. You probably wanted to suggest that the TO weapons were to be taken from TO warehouses and placed into JNA warehouses. Yes, there was an order to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. You're absolutely right. I think that's what I said or maybe I didn't or there was an interpretation mistake, but you're exactly right. I was interested in TO weapons being taken from TO warehouses and placed into JNA warehouses. Could we look at -- briefly at Exhibit 409, please, on our screens. Thank you. Maybe if we could just zoom in on the top half of the document for the witness. Yes. That's fine. Mr. Peric, this is the order that we were just talking about, right? This is the order to take control of the TO weapons and put them in JNA supply dumps and depots; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What's the date at the top of this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 14th of May, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And if we could just -- I'm not sure if it's at the bottom of the B/C/S or -- anyhow, at the end of this document, if you could scroll down, please, all the way to the bottom. I guess we need to go to the next page. Or, well, what I'm interested in is the signature line. So it's the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's right there underneath. The signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I didn't see that. Yes. Thank you. This is signed by Blagoje Adzic, the chief of the SFRY General Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You said yesterday that this order was carried out but only partially, only to a lesser extent. But it wasn't particularly clear that the time-frame you were talking about. In fact, although this order might have been less successfully implemented in Slovenia, in Croatia it was actually very thoroughly implemented and the JNA was able to take control of most of the Croatian Territorial Defence weapons. Right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were to orders, in fact. There is this order for the TO weapons to be placed into JNA warehouses, since, under the defence law of the SFRY, the TO was the second component of the armed forces under a unified command. In order to prevent any misuse, and given the fact that TO warehouses, to all practical intents, were secured to a lesser degree, in order to prevent any misuse of those weapons an order was given to remove those from TO warehouses to JNA warehouses where better security could be provided. Secondly, this is not about the return of weapons. There is another order from January 1991 for weapons to be returned that had been removed by force from JNA warehouses and other such places. And it was an order for those specific weapons to be returned, or rather handed over. This is an order of a quite different nature as compared to the one dated 1991. I was talking about the first one when I said that I only symbolic amounts of weapons were eventually returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. You were talking about the January 1991 order when you said only symbolic amounts of weapons were returned, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Precisely. Yes. Yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But the May 1990 order was successfully implemented in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And you referred to some reasons why you say this order was made. In fact, this order from the JNA to take control of TO weapons was done to control those weapons in the case of an attempted secession. Essentially this order was disarming the republic TOs in a sense, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why that would be tantamount to what you are suggesting. The only reason this was done was to ensure a better security regime and to prevent those weapons from being misused.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, this order was made over the objection of Slovenian and Croatians, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand. You mean that they opposed this proposal for the weapons from the TO warehouses to be removed or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's right. That's what I meant. This was -- Slovenians and Croatians in the leadership, the Yugoslav leadership at the time, opposed this. They objected to it but it was ordered anyhow.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the Yugoslav leadership opposing this order. What I do know is that there was opposition to this order by Croatia and Slovenia. They were opposing this order. I don't know about the federal leadership, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. We can take this document off the screen and if we could please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Can I ask before we take it off the screen. In the original B/C/S version I see this is a telex, isn't it, and there is no real signature. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All there is is an abbreviation by his own hand. But there is no original signature, if that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Just for the record. And this paper, this document has a lot of handwritten additions, remarks, signs. Do you want to clarify that with the witness, Mr. Black? Or is it not relevant maybe?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I don't believe it is important, and I haven't -- I have no reason to think the witness knows anything about those markings, although I could ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, these markings that you see on the page, you don't know anything about those, do you, about who made those markings or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whoever received the order, whichever official it was that received the order, I would be happy to say who. It's just initialled. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Can you read this handwritten additions? Or are they -- yes, there is some -- some handwriting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do my best. "Pursuant to this order, write down our own order and forward to corps commands and the republican TO staff, deadline 20th of May, 1990, by 1200 hours." The marking is NS. This means Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your help. And please, you can go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Sorry for taking your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No problem, Your Honour. Thank you. I would just note a translation of that does appear in the English version, that handwritten note is there. I appreciate the clarification on signature. I had misspoken and said it was signed by Adzic, but that is not what the document says, so I appreciate that, Your Honour. Thank you. Could we now see Exhibit 476 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You would like to see it before we take the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thanks, I had not noticed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Okay. Thank you so much. If it is convenient for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. We will take the break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, a few minutes before we took our break, we were talking about this May 1990 order, and you said -- I asked you whether it was done to disarm the republics and the republic TOs and you said that you didn't know why it would be tantamount to what I was suggesting. You said the only reason this was done was to ensure a better security regime and to prevent those weapons from being misused. Now, I would like to show you a passage from Exhibit 476 in this case. If we could see that, please. In English we'll be looking at page 131, the ERN is 03022947. In B/C/S it's 01157807. So if we could turn to that page, please. Mr. Peric, while we're waiting, Borisav Jovic was the acting chairman of the SFRY Presidency in the latter half of 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What's the title of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: This is the -- a book. It's Borisav Jovic's diary. I can't remember the title, actually, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Well, this document says last days of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It goes up to page 102 in the English, so we can't get to 131.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the bottom of each page, it should have a number, I believe. Because these are excerpts from a book. This is very similar to the situation we faced yesterday. This was a book that went into evidence, and so both sides proposed excerpts essentially and they were translated and everything. Perhaps the best way, Your Honour, the ERN number on the English page I'm interested in is 03022947. And in B/C/S it's 01157807. So if we can forward to that page, please. I'm sorry, Your Honour, I didn't realise this technical difficulty would be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The problem is not with technology. I think the problem is with the pagination. We just don't have --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Are you not able to find the page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And we don't have 03022947 either. It ends at 03022817. That's the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm informed by my colleague what is up on the English is the page that I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: It seems to be page 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It does, just to confirm, have the ERN at the top right-hand corner 03022947. Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes. Page 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Excellent. Thank you. It's the passage from the 17th of May, 1990, that I'm interested in. Thank you very much to the court ushers. We now have it on B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, this is from the published diary of Borisav Jovic. If you'll look with me at the entry for the 17th of May, 1990, he says, maybe I should just it out slowly: "We take measures to ensure that weapons are taken from civilian Territorial Defence depots in Slovenia and Croatia and transferred to military depots. We will not permit Territorial Defence weapons to be misused in any conflicts or for forcible secession. Practically speaking, we have disarmed them. Formally this was done by the head of the General Staff, but it was actually under our order. Extreme reaction by the Slovenes and Croatians but they have no recourse." Now having seen this entry from Borisav Jovic's diary, do you now accept that this order in May 1990 was done to disarm the republics in the case of an attempt at forcible secession?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the reasoning of the leadership itself. I don't know. I've not been aware of that so far, nor have I read Jovic's memoirs but it must be this way then. All I know is that the warehouses in which these weapons were being kept were poorly guarded and not in line with the prevailing regulations. I thought the main reason for doing that was security.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. But you accept now, having seen this document, that in fact there was another reason to disarm the republic TOs?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not my place to accept anything. If this is something that is being stated for the record here by the chairman of the Presidency or any of its members, then it probably must be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You would accept, wouldn't you, that Borisav Jovic by virtue of his position at the time would have had better information on this issue than you did, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm done with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a question to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was it your knowledge that in fact this order was applicable to all the territories, all the republics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what I knew was in relation to the 5th Army. I know that we received that order. I'm talking about the headquarters of the 5th Military District, and I don't know about any of the others. I simply didn't have that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I've got this document on the screen that I have control over and I'm not able to go back to -- on the other screen to previous evidence. But I thought you had indicated, or the question had been that the territorial authorities -- I beg your pardon. The republics were having their Territorial Defence forces being disarmed in all the territories. And I thought you said, yes, this was being done because of secure preservation of these weapons in the JNA depots. Didn't you refer to all of the republics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I only had Croatia in mind, no one else. I simply didn't know whether the order applied to all the other republics. I know that it was received in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: We're done with that document now, I believe. Mr. Peric, just to go back for one moment to the January 1991 order. And you explained a few minutes ago that was a different order from the May 1990 one. This was about return of weapons from -- that had been distributed to paramilitary groups. Am I recalling that correctly, the January 1991 order?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I remember and what I believe is that this was sometime after the Spegelj film was shown. I think after the 26th of January. There was an agreement to do just this, to try to retrieve all these weapons that, in different ways, had ended up in the hands of some people by illegal means, or by illegal input. That sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. I just wanted to make sure we're talking about the same order. You said yesterday that the Croatian authorities, and actually today as well, that the Croatian authorities didn't act on that and only a very small portion of weapons were actually returned, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the time back in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you know?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A very small portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you know that Milan Martic and the Krajina authorities also chose not to act on that January 1991 order, even though Milan Martic had informed JNA General Vasiljevic that they would do so. Did you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that. Being as I was a member of the army, I did not have access to this type of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Let me continue a little bit with -- following in chronological order. You mentioned Plitvice earlier. It's true that right -- I'm correct that around Easter of 1991 there was fighting between Croatia and Serb policemen in Plitvice, right? That's the incident that you are also referring to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that was late in March. Perhaps the 1st of March or in late March 1990. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And after that fighting erupted between the two sides, the JNA stepped in as a buffer and that was sort of how that fighting was resolved. Do you remember that? Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: On the 1st and 2nd of May, 1991, there was fighting in another part of Croatia and in Borovo Selo, which I believe is in eastern Slovenia. Do you know about that fighting in the beginning of May?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, a Serb was killed in Borovo Naselje. And then there was a riot, people started rioting in Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And there was actually conflict between Croatian and Serb policemen in Borovo Selo, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about what was behind those clashes. An ethnic Serb had been murdered. The population was unsettled. There was some unrest outside the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is insofar as my information was accurate. This was not something that was in the remit of the 5th Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me just --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just telling you about what I learned from the media. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. And I was really just interested in the fact that there was fighting there. And then again the JNA stepped in sort of as a buffer between the two sides. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And in this particular instance at least the effect of that JNA intervention was to consolidate the Serb control over the police station issue. Right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not aware of that, because I was not involved in these events. What I learned about them was what I heard or learned over the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, maybe more generally, it's true, isn't it, that even at this part of 1991, the first half of 1991, one of the JNA's goals at that stage was to protect the Serb nation in Croatia and to enable it to consolidate and militarily organise itself. Right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could not put it in those terms, that this was one of the goals of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, let me --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army was placed in a very uncomfortable situation as a buffer; you yourself put it in those terms. To me, as a professional soldier, this was puzzling. I didn't know what the -- what they were aiming at. To the Croatian people, we were the Yugoslav Chetnik army. Serbs on the other side were accusing us of not protecting them but rather protecting the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We found ourselves in a very ungrateful situation at the time because we were supposed to separate the two sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Let me again have you look at a document, and this is Exhibit 24 in evidence in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours, I will see if I can't give an e-court page number, but for the time being it's page 68 in English, which bears the ERN 00362704. That's page 126 in B/C/S, 00359490. It is page 9 of the e-court numbering. So it's a little confusing, because we have now three sets of numbers. But in the English it is page 9 of the e-court numbering, and at the bottom you will see the page number and the ERN that I just mentioned. In the B/C/S it is page 9 as well. Exactly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, Veljko Kadijevic was the SFRY federal secretary for All People's Defence at this time in 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What you're looking at now is a section from his book called "My View of the Breakup," which was published in Belgrade in 1993. And if we could scroll up just slightly so that we can see the top of the page in B/C/S, please. There. That's fine. Actually, it can go down a little bit. If we can see as much text as possible. Perfect. Do you see there, Mr. Peric, there's just one sentence by itself that says: "There were two phases in the armed fighting in Croatia." Do you see that on the screen?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Then the paragraph right below that explains that the first phase spanned the period from the first armed attacks on Serbs and the Serbian Krajina region to the end of the summer of 1991. So that's what Kadijevic means by the first phase in the armed fighting in Croatia. And now if you skip the next two paragraphs, so it would actually be on the right-hand side of the B/C/S version, there's a paragraph which begins -- it's right at the top, I think. It begins: "The aimed concept and plan for deployment of the JNA." Do you see that? If you look at the second sentence of that paragraph, it says: "Taking all this into account, the JNA's goal in the first phase of armed fighting in Croatia was to protect the Serb nation in Croatia against attack by armed Croat formations and to enable it to consolidate and militarily organise itself for defence." Then it continues with other goals. But having read -- having now seen this portion from Kadijevic's book, you would agree with me that that was one of the JNA's goals at that time, even before the end of the summer of 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this was indeed the goal, the way it is formulated here, then unfortunately the JNA failed to achieve it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, whether or not they achieved it or not, that was one of the goals here, at least according to Veljko Kadijevic. Right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were the ones to set it. I didn't do that. I see it now for the first time. I haven't been reading Veljko Kadijevic's memoirs because it was partly through his memoirs that he tried to justify some of his own failures.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But you're not doubting what's written here, that we just looked at, are you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So you're saying that he wrote this here in order to justify his own failures?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How would what we have just talked about justify Kadijevic's failures? I've focused, you know, specifically on this part that we had just looked at, about the JNA's goals up until the summer of 1991.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Kadijevic's position was such that he had to invest more efforts in order for the JNA to fulfil its constitutional obligations. It had not fulfilled any of its constitutional duties. The protection of territorial integrity of the country and the protection of the constitutional order, none of these tasks that were stipulated in the constitution were in fact fulfilled by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not asking you about the failures of the JNA or Kadijevic. What I really wanted to focus you on is, you know, this part of the book that we looked at, that's accurate, right? You can't explain that as some sort of, something created by Kadijevic to justify his failures. Just that specific part. Not in general. But the specific part that we looked at.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At my operational level, because you have the tactical operations and strategic levels in the army, at my operational level, operations level, I was not able to realise that this was the strategic goal that the JNA should organise and enable the Serb people to organise themselves and defend themselves; in other words, that the JNA should prepare them for a war against Croatia. At my own level, I did not have this impression, that we were tasked with preparing the Serb people for their own defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. But certainly whatever you think about his failings, you accept that Kadijevic, by virtue of his position, he knew more about the overall goals and policies of the JNA than you did at a lower level, right? He knew more about these issues than you did?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't discuss his knowledge or whether he, by the nature of things, knew them. I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his last remark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Will you please repeat your last remark, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how much he, Kadijevic, knew at this strategic level or whether he knew these matters. But what I said was that all his knowledge could do him no good, in view of the fact that the army failed to fulfil its constitutional obligations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Peric, again, let's not talk about whether or not they fulfilled its constitutional obligations. You're not seriously questioning that the SFRY federal secretary for All People's Defence, didn't know about JNA goals and policies, are you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he knew, why weren't these matters then carried out? As an officer --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No, let me ask you --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I swore I was going to defend the socialist --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You keep changing the question to implementation. But I'm asking you about goals and policies. And Kadijevic, by virtue of his position, must have known more about the JNA's goals and policies than you did, right? Can't you accept that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you're asking me to discuss about the matters that Mr. Kadijevic knew or didn't know. I'm telling you that he must have known nothing, in view of the fact that the whole country fell apart and his duty was to protect it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Can I ask a question. The witness made clear enough that he was on a different level and that his own knowledge derives from this operational level and not -- distinguishing that from the strategic level, where he could not say anything except now from hindsight, some speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it seems to me that he won't accept that the federal secretary knew more about policy than he did. He said that he knew things from the operational level, and the next question then is, okay, is it fair to say that the federal secretary would have known more. And he won't answer that question for me, it seems to me. That's the only question that I want an answer to right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I have problems with such an issue. To give testimony on as it is speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think it is speculation, because this is a career JNA officer. He has his place in the hierarchy. Of course there is someone at the top of the hierarchy, and it would seem a JNA officer would know whether or not someone at the top of the hierarchy better understands the goals and policy than he did below. And if that's the case he could say yes, or he could say I don't know. But that is not what he says. He continually changes the subject and tries to talk about implementation or satisfaction of constitutional obligations, and he won't answer me about goals and policies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just jump in here? What is remarkable about this point is that a little earlier, when we talked about the other leader, the author, this witness readily accepted that by virtue of that leader's position he would have known more than he himself did. And if it was easy to answer that question, I don't see why it is difficult to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: It's a parallel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is exactly the same question. Parallel situation. They're both -- they are both his seniors. And they're exposed to more information than he was and he can just easily say if he accepts or doesn't accept, like he did with the first one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Sorry. By implication, though, he seems to be saying that he should have known "more than me" about based on the end product. In reality, it does not appear as if he knew and understood. But ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The end product has nothing to do with the objectives of the JNA. If my objective is to go to Belgrade and I failed to catch the plane that must take me there, that does not change my objective. You can't say because I failed to get to Belgrade, therefore my objective was not to get to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: But can't we maybe go back to this order, as it is actually -- expressly referring to the tasks laid out by the federal secretary for national defence at the military council session of 27th of April, 1990. This is the basis expressed in the order. And maybe you can ask the witness if he knows about this session, or -- which would give more information about the background of the order. Otherwise we have just his diary or his memoirs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, I don't think this relates to a particular order. I'm not aware of a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: In the order it is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Is that Exhibit 409 you mean, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Because I'm actually talking about now up until the summer of 1991. So more than a year has passed since the time of that order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Sorry. You were talking about 1991, of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Perhaps a suggestion is just if the witness can answer, as Judge Nosworthy suggested, whether or not by virtue of Kadijevic's position he should have had more information about the JNA goals and policies than the witness did. Mr. Peric, can you answer that question? Or actually, Your Honour, is that an acceptable course?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I believe you were addressing the Presiding Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black is addressing your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it would be. Because I think "should have been" from that answer, you could move to the next position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is your original question "should have" or is your original question "did he"?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did he. That's the question that we really want him to answer. And I really think -- that was just a suggestion. I think the witness should answer the question that was been put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I mean the witness answered it with respect to the other leader. I'm sure he can answer it with respect to this leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, do you remember the question or would you like me to put it to you again?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, if the question could be put to me again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Certainly. I'm happy to. You would accept, would you not, that Kadijevic, by virtue of his position, knew more than you did about the goals and policies of the JNA at that time. And I'm talking about up until the summer of 1991.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
