utterances.text: By virtue of his position, the way I understand the chain of command and subordination, he probably should have had wider range and more sources of information than I did. I do accept that he did have more information than I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You testified yesterday about an agreement in July of 1991 that ended the war in Slavonia -- excuse me, Slovenia. That was the so-called Brioni agreement, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Slovenia, yes. In Slovenia. Not Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's exactly right. That was the Brioni agreement; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And the context in which that agreement was made was that Croatia and Slovenia had declared independence on the 25th of June, 1991, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Slovenia made this declaration on independence at that time. I'm not sure about Croatia, whether there this declaration was made at the same time or later on. This is a political issue, when the declarations were made. I know that Slovenia passed this declaration of independence on the 25th of June. I'm not sure whether Croatia did it at that date. I believe it was later. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: All right. Well, do you remember that the Brioni agreement, which ended the war in Slovenia on the 7th of July, after ten days of fighting in Slovenia, another provision of that agreement was that both Slovenia and Croatia would suspend implementation of independence for three months. There was going to be a moratorium on independence. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the agreement itself. Although it was referred to along the chain of command where it was stated that purportedly a truce had been achieved with Slovenia. I know the matters which arose from the agreement, that was that the border crossings were being toured and sealed. We told us to have the men ready to occupy every third border post, because that was purportedly the agreement with Slovenia. However, this was -- the implementation of it was interrupted, and I cannot really tell you or give you an interpretation of the Brioni agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. And if you don't know about this provision of the Brioni agreement you can just say so, that you didn't know about that one.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But I guess, you do -- you would agree with me that after Slovenia --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. After Slovenia declared independence, then there was ten days of fighting between Slovenian forces and the JNA; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Just one clarification. Yesterday when you were talking about the fighting in Slovenia, you said -- and I will quote it. It's actually from transcripts 7818. You said the Slovene forces took advantage of this and they fired mercilessly at those children who were sitting ducks because they had no orders -- because they had orders not to respond. And it's just a point of clarification, sir. When you referred to "children" there, you were talking about JNA soldiers, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Let me add this: These clashes were not between the JNA and the Slovene TO. This was an outright attack against the JNA and the JNA had the orders not to respond to the fire. Fighting implies that you have two sides that are active players. This was an attack against the JNA units, with the ultimate goal of humiliating the JNA --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, let me interrupt you --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- before the domestic and international public.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm not intending to go into the details again about this because you testified about it yesterday. But you don't deny that there was, you know, weapons fired from both sides and in fact people from both sides died. JNA people died and Slovenians died, didn't they, in this ten-day war.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying the following. The general order given to the units that were deployed to Slovenia was that they should not open fire, that they should complete their mission without opening fire. However, under the rules of engagement of the JNA, there is one provision which clearly states that where a military unit is attacked, the unit shall open fire without anyone's order or approval. They were forced to defend themselves along some axes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about that. I'm not trying to talk about who started the fighting. But there was fighting between them, right? Even if it's as you say that it was only in defence to attacks, but even accepting that, there was fighting between the JNA and the Slovenian forces, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The definition of combat is far more complex.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yeah, I don't need a technical definition. I just want -- I mean, you don't dispute that they fired their guns at each other and people died on both sides, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were such instances, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And in Croatia, which I will submit to you also declared independence on the 25th of June, 1991, Croatia witnessed, in a sense, the fighting in Slovenia. They saw what happened to Slovenia after it tried to declare independence, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they most certainly did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And so my question for you is: In light of everything that happened, starting with the issue or the order issued in May 1990 to seize the TO weapons, all the different conflicts that we've discussed, the war in Slovenia, isn't it fair to say that by blockading JNA facilities Croatia was really trying to re-establish its control over weapons and to avoid a war with the JNA such as that that took place in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Far from it. I can't agree with you. I can't agree that by imposing blockade on barracks they wanted to prevent war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: By the way, military barracks and weapons depots and military convoys, those are all legitimate military targets, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Legitimate for whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Legitimate in combat, under the laws of war. Those are legitimate targets. They're not civilian targets that you can't hit. They're legitimate military targets, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are legitimate when you fight legitimate forces. But what were the legitimate forces of Croatia? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me continue a little bit. And now we're focusing on the period that starts in August of 1991. From that point on, you would agree with me, would you not, that the JNA role radically changed, and it wasn't about providing a buffer, it was really about open support for the Serb side of the conflict in Croatia. Right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In August? No. In August its role was still that of a buffer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In your view, did the role change; and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It changed by the very fact that attacks were mounted on garrisons, organised blind attacks that ensued after blockades on barracks. There was disarming of soldiers, looting of depots and they had to defend themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Excuse me. In what time-frame are you talking about? When did this start? When did this change in role begin?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you know that Milan Martic had publicly stated, even in July of 1991, that his SAO Krajina police force had cooperation with the JNA, that they were assisting one another in a fight against a common enemy; in other words, Croatia. Were you aware of those public statements?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Were you aware that the JNA and SAO Krajina police fought together under joint command in Kijevo in August of 1991? In fact, Milan Martic personally participated in that attack, as did Ratko Mladic of the JNA? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know there was some commotion about Kijevo. Who cooperated with whom is something that I was not privy to. I did not have access to such information. All I could learn was from the media reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What about in Drnis in September 1991? Did you know that the JNA fought together with SAO Krajina TO and police in Drnis in September 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you know that the JNA and SAO Krajina TO and police fought together around Saborsko and Skabrnja in November of 1991? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: November 1991? In my position, I did not have the possibility of following what was going on along the Dalmatian coast, in the Dalmatian area. I know from media reports that there were some conflicts involving the TO, the police, but I couldn't tell you who did what to whom, because I didn't follow that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, speaking more generally, then, I guess, and you said yourself that there was a change in the JNA role by September of 1991. Isn't it true that that was, it was a radical change in the sense that instead of creating a buffer, then the JNA actually took the side of the Serb -- the Serbs in Croatia and fought to defend the Serb national interest in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's exactly where the problem lies, that the JNA practically as a result of synchronised action of secessionist forces became nobody's army. The Yugoslavia they knew was broken up, and there was no state standing behind that army anymore. They were left to their own devices, its units had to defend themselves and their own. And the Serbs would not have suffered such great losses from Croatian paramilitary forces if the JNA had indeed been protecting them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm not 100 per cent clear on your answer. Again, you talk about what you think you can infer from implementation. But do you accept that by the end of the summer of 1991 the JNA's goal, its role in the conflict had radically changed and the JNA had now taken the side of the Serbs and was protecting Serb national interest in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think you could put it that way. The JNA still played the role of a buffer, a separating force. But it also had to defend its own units, its own equipment from all sorts of dangers and threats. There were territories in which the JNA protected Croats as well. Not only Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could look again at Exhibit 24, please. I'm actually interested in pages 49 to 50 in English. It's 92 to 93 in the B/C/S. So in B/C/S that's the sixth page of the e-court. And in English it's pages 6 and 7 in the e-court. Actually, if we could start there at the sixth page in English. I believe it is on the same page in B/C/S. Or, no. Actually, it begins on page 92 in B/C/S, right, on the sixth page.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Peric -- I'm sorry, can we go back to a bigger view of this? I just want to ask your assistance, actually, sir. There are a couple of paragraphs beginning with italicised words, and one of them says "fourth," then a little further down you see "the second phase," "the third phase." Do you see those on this page?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Serbian, it's page 92, 93.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks very much. And on that page 92 on the left-hand side, in the middle of that paragraph --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: -- I think there's a sentence that says: "Three phases characterised the development of the situation and deployment of the armed forces was conceived accordingly." Again, sir, this is again the book by Veljko Kadijevic. So now that you know what he's talking about in terms of the three phases, skip along to the paragraph that begins "the third phase." And that's on the right hand page, page 93 in B/C/S. The first sentence is quite long.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The second one begins: "At the beginning of this phase." There's talking about -- actually, maybe I should go to the beginning of that paragraph. It explains that: "The third phase began when Germany, acting through the European community, openly took over management of the Yugoslav crisis." These are Kadijevic's words. "...compelled Slovenia and Croatia to accelerate their secessation by having them apply force." So this is talking about basically beginning at the end of the summer of 1991. That references there are to the declarations of independence and the recognition by Germany. The second paragraph -- second sentence of that paragraph is the one I am interested in. It says: "At the beginning of this phase, the armed forces' task radically changed and was to, 1, defend the Serb nation in Croatia and its national interests; 2, pull JNA garrisons out of Croatia; 3, gain full control of Bosnia-Herzegovina ..." and it continues with the tasks. But that first -- first part of this new radically changed task was to defend the Serb nation in Croatia and its national interests. That accurately reflects what happened to the JNA in the end of the summer of 1991, right, it had this radical change in its task. Now it was defending Serb national interests.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please rephrase your question, because I didn't quite understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. It may not have been a very clear question. Let me say it again. At the end of the summer of 1991, Kadijevic is correct, isn't he, that the task of the JNA radically changed and it became, at least in part, about defending the Serbs in Croatia and the Serb national interests in Croatia. That happened, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not agree with this, because that's not how things were. It sounds nice as it is written in Kadijevic's book, but it is not correct. Croatia practically ceased, simply robbed 50 per cent of the JNA. The officers, conscripts, they pulled them out of JNA units then they took over barracks, looted weapons, looted the trains, leaving Slovenia, and there was little left of the JNA units in Croatia. Furthermore, Croatia took over the military files of conscripts that should have reinforced the JNA, and even then they had more manpower and more weaponry than the JNA units in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, I just want to -- whatever it is that you say about JNA units in Croatia, the JNA as the federal army still existed, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It existed, but it was weakened. It was reduced to a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The JNA had been one of the strongest armies in Europe before 1990; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how it rated, but maybe. Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, you served your career in the JNA. There is no reason not to be modest. The JNA prided itself on being a strong army, comparable, I think many people said to the NATO-type armies, right? This was one of the strongest armies in Europe.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am proud of it, and I indeed believe it was, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And so certainly when you look at the JNA in all of Yugoslavia you're not suggesting that it was -- that the Croatian -- the new Croatian armed forces were more powerful than the JNA, are you? You're not saying that, I don't think.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am saying this: Already by November, especially after the fall of garrisons in Croatia in September and October, the JNA was weakened. The JNA units in Croatia were weakened to such an extent that Croatian paramilitary forces outnumbered them five to one, or even ten to one, according to some estimates, as a result of the breakup and crushing of army units. Therefore, it is not fair to say that there were some powerful JNA units there in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Before I got sidetracked on that issue, we were talking about JNA goals. And is it possible that you were misled about the actual goals of the JNA leadership? I mean, given what we saw --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what sense do you mean you were sidetracked?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, forget about that. The question -- my question for you now is, you know, we looked at the diary of Borisav Jovic, and you said that you weren't aware of the things that were said there. Then we looked at a couple of excerpts from Kadijevic's book, and you said that you didn't agree with what was written there about JNA goals. But isn't it possible that you were misled about the goals of the JNA leadership?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a soldier, in my military career, I was taught very different things to what happened in 1991 and 1990 and in the beginning of the 1990s generally speaking. I firmly believed in a united Yugoslavia. I was proud to be a part of those forces, of the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army. And when secessionist forces appeared in the political arena, we were convinced that there was no way these forces would become so powerful as to be able to tear away two republics from Yugoslavia, and I admit that I was an idealist, yes, just an idealist.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Right. And aside from what you felt and what other soldiers and officers in the JNA felt, the leadership of the JNA abandoned those goals of unity and brotherhood, didn't they, in 1991. And they abandoned that and they took the side of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand. Which leadership?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The leadership of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They abandoned those goals, well, of course. In the JNA, too, there were people working for the interests of the secessionist forces. At the very top it is the misfortune of both the previous and the present union that there was always treason in 1941, in 1991. It seems to be our curse.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And the JNA leaders that abandoned those goals of unity and brotherhood, they weren't just what you call secessionist forces. It wasn't just Croats and Slovenes, it was also Serbs. In 1991 the Serb JNA leadership abandoned those goals of unity and brotherhood, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You couldn't say that they abandoned it equally. People who were in key positions in the General Staff of the JNA, like Anton Tus and some others like him, sided immediately with the secessionist forces. I don't know of a single Serb who supported secessionism. I never saw anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, you also testified yesterday a little bit about JNA personnel policy and things like that. It's true, isn't it, that by the end of 1991 the vast majority of senior officers in the JNA were all Serb or Montenegrin ethnicity, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've said already that relative to the total population of the then Yugoslavia, it would have been natural if at least 50 per cent were Serbs, because there were almost 50 per cent Serbs in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, let me --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been natural if there were 50 per cent Serbs among the officers and the leadership, but it was not the case. The leadership of the JNA was really ethnically very mixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, I'm talking about the --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbs did not prevail anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm talking about the end of 1991, okay? By the end of 1991 in Croatia, certainly of combat units, almost all of the commanding officers were Serb or Montenegrin; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1991? No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: By the end of 1991, you still dispute that? Even though we're talking about the end of 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do dispute that. That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me ask you: From August 1991 to November of 1991, you were stationed at the JNA forward command post in Slunj; correct? I believe you testified about that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: At the time that you were in Slunj, JNA forces there cooperated with or acted in coordination with SAO Krajina TO forces and police forces by forming temporary operational groups or tactical groups, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there existed tactical groups made up entirely of JNA units. I didn't know about any other units being involved. I left Slunj on the 19th of August [as interpreted], as I've said before, and at that stage we were still a buffer, a separation force. And for the most part, the key activity of the army on the forward command post in Slunj was to escort the transports of equipment and weapons leaving Slovenia. There was the key task of the command of the 5th Army District. We wondered, we the officers --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. Just first one correction. The translation we got is that you left Slunj on the 19th of August, but it was the 19th of November, 1991 that you left Slunj, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Around the 20th November we left the forward command post and went to Mount Kozara.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And you said that you were aware of, I don't remember -- tactical groups, you said. Were you aware of the Operational Group 3 that was in existence at that time, in October and November of 1991, in that area of Slunj? Does that ring a bell to you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was in Plitvice. I don't remember exactly, but I think it was in Plitvice.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. What about Tactical Group 2, which was created on the 23rd of October, 1991? Do you remember that tactical group being created?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I know there was a check-point in Slunj and a check-point in Plitvice, as far as tactical groups are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, this tactical group was commanded by Colonel Cedomir Bulat of the JNA. Does that help you remember about Tactical Group 2?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That group remained with Colonel Bulat. After we left Slunj and moved on command post to Mount Kozara, that tactical group remained behind in Slunj, together with Colonel Bulat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And that tactical group contained JNA forces and SAO Krajina TO forces and the TO forces were reinforced with police units. Do you remember all that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the composition of that group. I didn't work on that. It was usually the Chief of Staff who decided that, together with the chief of operations. I did not work on the composition of that group. I can't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe it is probably a convenient time for a break for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is indeed. We will take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black. How much longer are you likely to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm conscious of time. Things went a little slower than I anticipated at the beginning. I think I will be most of the session. I don't think I will take up the whole day but it's possible. Most of the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, you joined the SAO Krajina TO in March of 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 1st of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And then you subsequently joined the SVK in December of 1992, and you served in the SVK up through 1995, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: During that entire time, you remained a member of the Yugoslav army and in fact you received your pay from the JNA and then subsequently the VJ; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. In that in early 1992, I made a statement to the effect that I was joining the Territorial Defence of the republic of the Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. But you made -- who did you make that statement to, to the effect you were joining the TO?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was required by the personnel service of the command of the military district.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Within the JNA, right, the personnel service of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And even after you made that statement to them, you were still actually part of the JNA and then the VJ, even though you were serving in the RSK, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And you received your salary from the JNA and then from the VJ; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yesterday you testified a little bit about the Vance Plan. So I'm going to ask you a few questions about the Vance Plan. It's correct, isn't it, that the Vance Plan had three principal aspects: The deployment of UN peacekeepers in the UNPAs, demilitarisation, and the return of refugees. Those were the three main points of the Vance Plan; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have occasion to see and read the plan, but I do believe that that is the gist of the plan, based on what I learned of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Now you testified yesterday that under the Vance Plan, in the event of a Croatian attack on Western Slavonia the JNA could step in to defend Western Slavonia. That's what you said yesterday. Am I right about that? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Purportedly such a provision was contained in the Vance Plan. As I said, I didn't have occasion to have the plan in my hands, but I was acquainted with the provision as guarantee of the safety of the Serb people in Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you remember how you heard about that specific part, about the JNA being able, under the Vance Plan, to step in to defend Western Slavonia? Did you hear about that in the media or through some other way?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first piece of information concerning the conflicts in Western Slavonia reached me on the 15th of August, 1991, when the forces of the Croatian MUP --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, let me just interrupt you, sorry.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- came into Okucani on APCs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Maybe you misunderstood my question. This purported provision, as you have said, of the Vance Plan, you know, that the JNA could step in to defend Western Slavonia in the event of an attack by Croatian forces, that particular provision that you say was purportedly in the Vance Plan, do you remember how you heard about that, specifically that provision, purported provision?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that from the commander of the Territorial Defence of Western Slavonia whose deputy I was, Colonel Cubric Jovo. He was the first TO commander in Western Slavonia. He took the position in March of 1992. I came to be his deputy. And he told me that the Vance Plan contained this provision, that in the event of Western Slavonia coming under attack from the Croatian forces, the JNA, or later the VJ, would step in to help them. I didn't have the opportunity to see the text of the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Would you accept that that was -- that may have been their interpretation, but that that actually wasn't contained in the Vance Plan? Is that a possibility?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, because as I said, I didn't have occasion to read the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And the reason I ask that is because in May of 1992 Croatia had been internationally recognised as an independent state and it was in fact a member of the United Nations. So it doesn't really make sense, does it, that the United Nations would enter an agreement which allowed the JNA to come into the territory of Croatia, a UN Member State. That doesn't really make sense, does it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Vance Plan was reached before the recognition of Croatia, as far as I know. In February or March already some of the first forces were deployed there. UNPROFOR forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, you're quite right about the timing of the Vance Plan. My question, I guess, and maybe you just can't answer this or you don't know, but it doesn't make sense that once Croatia was internationally recognised and that it was a UN Member State, it doesn't make sense that the UN would allow the JNA to come into the territory of Croatia for combat purposes, does it? If you don't know, I understand; you can just say so.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. But I believed that the United Nations were the body that had the mandate to protect the Serb population in Western Slavonia and that they were supposed to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. As we mentioned just a moment ago, one of the central provisions of the Vance Plan was demilitarisation within the UNPAs, right? In and sides actually were supposed to demilitarise. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And one of the specific parts of that demilitarisation was that TO members were supposed to wear civilian clothes; they weren't supposed to ware their uniforms anymore. That was part of that demilitarisation, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. And we wore civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Right. You testified yesterday that you said senior officers of the TO wore civilian clothes. Is your testimony that only --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: -- only the senior officers or all members of the TO stopped wearing uniforms and started wearing civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All. All of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could, I would like you to look with me at a document. It bears the ERN R 0128678 to 8679.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think -- we may not have a B/C/S translation of this document yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do we?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No, we don't, so I would request that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Peric, this is only in English, so I'm going to have to lead you through it. This document refers to a meeting on the 11th of March, 1993 between UNPROFOR and Serb authorities in Okucani. In paragraph 2, it says the following. It says: "The Serb side was represented by the deputy of the new Territorial Defence force commander (Colonel Slobodan Peric, chief of Okucani police), Mr. Ostrolucanin, police liaison officer with UNPROFOR, Mr. Zrnic, and the chairman of the so-called Regional Council of Western Slavonia, Mr. Vitez." The wording of this is not particularly clear to me. Do you remember attending a meeting with UNPROFOR on the 13th of March, 1993 or was it your deputy who attended? Can you remember that? I'm sorry, the meeting was on the 11th of March, I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many such meetings, I don't know how many, and it is quite possible that I attended the meeting. I can't rule that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. I... In number 4, it talks about the agenda for this meeting and it says: "The agenda included only two items: (a) new procedures introduced by the local Serb police for refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina coming through the Sava Bridge; and (b) violations of CVP," or Cyrus Vance Plan, "(wearing military uniforms) in Serb-controlled areas." Do you remember attending any meetings with UNPROFOR in which one of the agenda items was the continued wearing of military uniforms by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall this specifically, because such meetings were normally held once weekly. I can't remember that the wearing of uniforms was specifically discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Not even at this specific meeting, but can you ever remember the continued wearing of military uniforms as a topic of discussion with UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have had several talks, specifically with the deputy commander for Sector West, who at the time was Colonel Devegar [phoen]. I can tell you that they accepted this as quite normal, after the setting up of the Serbian army of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I don't quite understand. What was it that they accepted as "quite normal"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The wearing of uniforms by our soldiers, officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page of this document on our screens. Mr. Peric, while we're waiting for it to turn, in fact UNPROFOR considered the continued wearing of military uniforms as a violation of the Vance Plan. It was a clear violation of the language of the Vance Plan, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in 1992. Later on this no longer posed a problem. As of the 1st of December, 1992, when the army of the Serbian Krajina was established, the wearing of uniforms no longer posed a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But the Vance Plan wasn't amended or revisited in December of 1992. Its provisions were still the same, and demilitarisation was still a central provision of the Vance Plan, wasn't it? Even in 1993 and afterwards.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The UNPA, this particular UNPA went as far as Grdzevac and Grubisno Polje. Why were the Croatian forces, then, allowed to enter the area wearing uniforms? This applied to them as much as it did to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, I don't -- I'm not disputing that it applied to both sides. Let's instead of talking about the Croatian forces, let's focus on the Serb forces, okay? In fact, actually let's look at the document, because in paragraph 7, it says that this meeting in March of 1993, the UNPROFOR sector commander emphasized that the continuing wearing of camouflage military uniforms by demobilised TDF members was in violation of a major provision of the Vance Plan, and urged the Serb side to comply with the Plan. Then in paragraph 8 it says: "The Serb side," it enumerates them, "the deputy TDF commander, Messrs. Vitez and Ostrolucanin, bluntly refused to comply with this provision of the Vance Plan citing orders from the Knin military command and the state of war declared in the so-called Republic of Srpska Krajina as an excuse." Actually, it goes on to say that again in paragraph 9 that the Serb side repeatedly refused to comply. That's true, isn't it? In 1993, and specifically in March of 1993, the SVK and the Serb side more generally was openly and repeatedly refusing to comply with the demilitarisation provisions of the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see who signed this document, but we wore uniforms because the other side, the Croatian side, was allowed to wear uniforms within the UNPA. Accordingly, we thought it quite natural for us to be allowed to do that, if the other side was allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So I guess, is it fair to say, then, that you thought you could violate the Vance Plan if the other side violated the Vance Plan? That was the position at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this be made an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number 936.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second. I just want to get clarity. Now, Mr. Witness, you say that you were justified in wearing the uniforms because was the other side was also wearing uniforms; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. Your Honour, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: A few minutes ago, when you answered to a question by Mr. Black, and you said: "Right, and we wore civilian clothes," you were not absolutely correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was talking about the period up to the 1st of December, 1992. In that period we wore civilian clothes. However, as of the 1st of December, 1992, when the Serbian army of Krajina was established, we started wearing uniforms. So this applied also to 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But the question to you had been: "And one of the specific parts of that demilitarisation was that TO members were supposed to wear civilian clothes. They weren't supposed to wear their uniforms anymore. That was part of the demilitarisation. Right?" And you said: "Yes, right, and we wore civilian clothes." It doesn't refer to any specific time. It refers to the entire time during which the Vance Plan was in place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You show me from that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stressed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You show me from that question and from your answer where you stressed that you were referring to a specific time. I have quoted to you the question and answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Black asked whether we wore civilian clothes, and I told him that under the Vance Plan we wore civilian clothes until the 1st of December, when the Serbian army of Krajina was set up. Because up to that point we were TO, and from that point onwards we were the SVK, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are not saying so in this answer that I have just quoted to you. You just said: "Right, and we wore civilian clothes." Full stop.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I stressed at the outset that this was the TO until the SVK was established on the 1st of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I won't take the matter any further. Yes, you may proceed, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: May I ask you, you will deliver a translation to this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, another way in which the RSK failed to comply with the demilitarisation provisions of the Vance Plan was by basically transforming the TO into RSK special police units, or PJM; correct? That happened during the first half of 1992, that the TO was transformed into special police units.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could not say that this was the case for all of the TO. It was just part of the TO men who joined the special police.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And in addition to personnel, actually weapons and other equipment were also transferred to the new special police units; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They wore sidearms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And other kinds of equipment too, right? There were -- for instance, there were cases where TO trucks would be repainted in a different colour and then they would be part of the special police units. Were you aware of things like that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We learnt that from Croatia. They transformed their police units into military units, but they just coloured -- they painted over the blue colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And then you did essentially the same thing in Western Slavonia. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did the same thing they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And, in fact, you made a reference to carrying sidearms, but the RSK special police units actually carried long weapons, too, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They only carried sidearms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You didn't know that the RSK special police had long weapons which they received from the JNA and from the RSK TO? Or do you say that that was not the case?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On orders, they carried sidearms whilst on duty. Whereas long weapons were stored in depots.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The United Nations itself concluded, didn't it, that the transformation of TO formations and JNA material and equipment into the RSK special police units, that that was a violation of the Vance Plan, of the demilitarisation provisions; isn't that right? Or if you don't know, you can say that as well.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, because I never set eyes on this Vance Plan. I didn't know. As for the violation of its provisions, they were violated by both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the Daruvar agreement from February of 1993? Maybe -- if I could give you a few more details it will help you. It's an agreement between officials of Western Slavonia and Croatia and it was negotiated in part by the -- for the Serb side by Veljko Dzakula, who was the regional president of the SDS and the deputy prime minister. Are you familiar with that agreement? You're smiling and nodding your head.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I am familiar with the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And the question -- the specific question that I have for you about the agreement is that it was rejected by the RSK leadership in Knin, right, and actually forced Mr. Dzakula out of office and smeared his reputation, and he was even arrested and accused of treason. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the Z-4 plan that was proposed, although never adopted in 1994? Do you remember hearing about that plan?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection because the Z-4 plan was not mentioned in the examination-in-chief, and I thought the cross-examination has to be related to the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, the cross-examination has to be related to the entire case, and they can -- the cross-examiner is perfectly entitled to ask him questions. It is a very open question to which the witness can say if he does or does not know. So the objection is overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, I'm not sure if we recorded your answer. Are you -- do you remember hearing about the Z-4 plan in 1994?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly heard of it and later I had occasion to even read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you know that me Milan Martic opposed the Z-4 plan in fact he refused even to look at it? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was beyond me. I couldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: One of the provisions of the Z-4 agreement would have provided for the reintegration of Western Slavonia into Croatia, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But the plan was never agreed and never adopted, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But generally two areas, two districts, Glina and Knin, Western Slavonia was not part of that plan. It was excluded. And I was concerned with Western Slavonia. In Western Slavonia, we were very bitter about the fact that it was simply thrown out of the plan, Z-4.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: When you say it was excluded, what you mean is that Western Slavonia was actually going to go back into Croatia. It was going to be reintegrated into Croatia, right? That was what the Z-4 proposal provided.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how the designers of the Z-4 plan imagined to reintegrate Western Slavonia into Croatia, but the plan was concerned with two districts, Glina and Knin. There was not a word about Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You also testified about a cease-fire agreement from March of 1994, and you said in fact that it was not honoured by the Croatian side but it was honoured by the RSK. Do you remember talking about that cease-fire agreement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In fact, like the Vance Plan, there were actually violations on both sides of the March 1994 cease-fire agreement; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were minor violations. They were not violated to such an extent as to be a burden to the public. Insignificant.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I guess -- are you saying that the violations on both sides were essentially minor violations that weren't grave enough to be a burden to the public? Or are you talking only about one side?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About both sides, until around the 20th of April, which is when the tensions around Western Slavonia started.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The 20th of April, 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Given what we've talked about, these various different proposals and agreements and the violations on both sides, by April or May 1995, Croatia really had no choice if it wanted to reintegrate Western Slavonia but to do so by force, right, because it was clear that the RSK leadership was firmly opposed to any negotiated solution for Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had a choice. However, it chose war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And the reason that the international community accepted the use of force by Croatia was essentially because of the repeated violations of the Vance Plan and the Serb side's refusal to seriously negotiate a peaceful resolution, right? That's why the international community accepted the use of force in May 1995.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The concept of international community is broad. There is a book by an author of the name Jelena Guskov called "The History of the Yugoslav Crisis" and it analyzes the overall crisis in the Yugoslav territory. The author is a member of the Russian Academy of Science, and the relevant part is pages 219 to 229.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm impressed by the specificity of your citation. I am just going to ask you to please keep this answer very brief because we do have some more ground to cover. So please don't get too involved. Just give us a brief answer to this, please, if you can.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tudjman said, in no uncertain terms about Krajina, that Croatia could have avoided war, but didn't want to avoid it. Therefore, Croatia supported the war option. And throughout that time, in March 1995, Tudjman promised to Holbrooke that he would not resolve the Krajina problem by use of military force. And he cheated Holbrooke basically. And you can read about that in the book by Karl Bilt "The Peace Mission."

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You testified yesterday a little bit about Operation Flash at the beginning of May 1995. And you said that according to rough figures, approximately 284 persons had been identified as killed in Operation Storm. My question is for you: Those numbers come from the Veritas organisation in Belgrade, right? Is that the source of those figures that you cited?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was the only one to collect such data including name and surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, you know that they actually received some of their data from the Croatian Commission on Missing Persons; that's one of the places where Veritas being got their information. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know their sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. You know you also referred to another figure. You said that you believed personally believed that the total number killed was 2.500 people. Do you remember telling us what? Did we get the --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said 1.200 in my estimate. 1.200 in my estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Well that's an important correction, because yesterday the transcript had read 2.500, but you meant to say 1.200? Where does that figure come from, that 1.200 figure?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a direct participant. I saw with my own eyes in Novi Varos village at least 100 victims. It's a village between the motorway and the Sava river. Second, out of the units and unit commanders who were withdrawing south of the Sava river, I received reports from the casualties and victims they saw. Let's say from Rajici to Bodegraj, there were more than 60 corpses lying by the road. In Medari, 38. Just to give you some examples. My rough estimate was around 1.200, especially in the north zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And that's your estimate based on the extrapolation of what you have just told us, and it's not something that's been confirmed by any organisation or other source of evidence that you can point us to; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Exhumation has not started yet in the territory of Sector West and we still don't know the exact figure, but I think my estimates will be justified.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In your testimony yesterday, Defence counsel showed to you two transcripts, and they were transcripts from meetings of Croatian President Tudjman with his advisors on the 29th and the 30th of 1995 [sic]. Do you remember looking at those two documents?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And the suggestion was that, based on those documents, it showed that Tudjman had staged the incident that provoked Operation Flash, or that justified Operation Flash. That was what was being suggested, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And Bobetko himself wrote in his book "All My Battles" that they had done certain things, as he put it, deep inside the territory; he meant on the Serbian side. And I know, for certain, because I was there on the motorway in the night of the 28th, that nobody in the Serbian Krajina units opened fire on Croatian vehicles. It was a Croat terrorist sabotage group that opened fire. And that is when our troops approached, because that motorway was in the territory under the protection of the UNPROFOR, and that's how the Croats arranged the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I want to talk to you about -- I want to focus on dates for a second. Because, you know, those transcripts were from the 29th and the 30th of April, 1995. But the incidents that sort of provoked or gave the justification for Operation Flash, those happened before the 29th and 30th, before those meetings, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean. In any case, Bobetko made it absolutely plain in his book that they had done certain things deep inside the territory, and we couldn't understand at the time how come there was gunfire on the motorway when our units were not there. They just took advantage of that incident, to use it as a pretext, as well as the killing of Tihomir Blagojevic at the petrol station in Gradiska.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: When was Tihomir - sorry, what was his last name? - Blagojevic, when was he killed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tihomir Blagojevic was killed around 1900 hours on the 28th of April at a petrol station in Nova Gradiska. He was stabbed to death.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you now to look at a document. It is Exhibit 99, if we could see this on our screens, please. Mr. Peric, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: This is a report on the causes and manner of the fall of Western Slavonia, and it is dated the 11th of July, 1995; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And the commission which compiled this report, the names are given right there on the first page. Number 2 is Colonel Slobodan Peric. That's you; right? You were a member of the commission?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could just look quickly at the last page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I understand something about the composition of that commission. Which one is the witness, number 1 or number 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I believe it is number 2. I will ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, on that first page there, as His Honour points out, there are two Slobodan Peric; the first Slobodan Peric, Minister of the Interior; and second, Colonel Slobodan Peric, Commander of the 18th Corps. Which one are you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Or are you both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, he is no relative of mine. He just happens to be a full namesake. He had been elected minister of the interior. I'm in no way related to him. It's just a coincidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Peric. At least now we know which one you are in this commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, now we're looking at the last page. Can you just confirm that in the second spot there, that's your signature where you signed this report?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The second spot or the third spot? Oh, second spot, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: This report was compiled based on statements or interviews from a number of people directly involved in these events, including Milan Martic himself and others; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Actually, if we could go back to the first page. Those people are listed at the beginning of the document, all the people who were consulted in compiling the report; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Here we go.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page, please. All right. Sir, Mr. Peric, that's a continuation of the list of names of people who were essentially consulted in compiling this report; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page in B/C/S, page 3, and it's on page 4 of the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Page?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Page 3 in B/C/S, Your Honours, and page 4 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, do you see there the heading number 1, "Why did western Slavonia fall?" Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And just below that it says: "Pursuant to the decision by the President of the Republic," and that's a reference to Milan Martic, "of 24 April 1995, the motorway was closed down for 24 hours, from 0600 hours on the 24th of April until 0600 hours on the 25th of April, 1995." And that's correct, isn't it, that's accurate, what it says?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The next paragraph down says: "During 25, 26 and 27 April 1995, Western Slavonia was visited by President Martic and Commander Celaketic. They held a number of meetings and public gatherings in which they stated that the situation around the motorway was going to become very complicated and that the SVK was ready to protect and defend Western Slavonia and even reclaim a part of occupied territory." That's also accurate, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Then the next paragraph, if you could just read that first line and then we will turn to the second -- the next page in B/C/S. The next paragraph explains, as you had just referred to a moment ago, that Tihomir Blagojevic, who was a Serb, he was killed at a petrol station on the 28th of April, 1995. He was killed by a Croat from his home village; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And after that, as it says in the report: "Several citizens of Croatian nationality were killed on the night between 28 and 29 April on the stretch of motorway passing through our territory. It is indicative that, to this day, our state authorities have not established who are the perpetrators of the killing of Croatian citizens on the motorway." That is also accurate, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a report that three were killed and four were wounded, and that the UNPROFOR transported the wounded to Nova Gradiska for treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And that all happened on the night between the 28th and the 29th of April; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 28th and the 29th. In fact the night of the 29th I was on the motorway myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And so it's impossible, isn't it, that Croatian President Tudjman, on the 29th and the 30th of April, could have staged these incidents that actually happened before that; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw what was written on that transcript and I didn't say anything about that. But I concluded, from what I read in Bobetko's book, that it was planned provocation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, actually, when you were asked to look at those transcripts, you said that that confirmed that Croatia had staged the incidents that justified Western Slavonia; right? That's what you had said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said they were using such means. In our territory, it's a very frequent manoeuvre that has been used very often, starting with incidents like Markale market in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. But you -- I take it you agree with me that at those meetings on the 29th and 30th, of which you saw the transcript, they could not possibly have been planning these incidents that took place before those meetings happened; right? I mean, as a matter of logic you agree with that.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Black, if Bobetko reported to Tudjman on the 25th of April that their forces were ready to attack Western Slavonia and had drawn close, you know what usually goes on before such an aggression: scouts, reconnaissance, et cetera. So I don't doubt for a moment that that part was orchestrated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, first I'm going to ask you to answer my question, which was: Those meetings on the 29th and 30th, they could not have been staging these incidents or even -- that appear here, that happened before the meetings, right? You agree with that? Don't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that it proves your point, because the bureaucracy and administration can change dates whenever they please. The date on a document doesn't mean much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If you accept that -- well, the dates in this report that we're looking at, these are accurate dates, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So unless someone has maliciously changed the dates on the transcripts that we looked at yesterday, if those meetings did in fact occur on the 29th and 30th, they couldn't have been staging these events that happened on the 20th -- 28th, excuse me, and into the 29th. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I follow my own common sense as a soldier who is often used to assessing situations, I think that that was a conversation that took place before and was placed in a post-dated transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So that's your explanation, that the dates of those transcripts must be wrong. Those conversations must have taken place before it actually says they did?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not exactly. I would say that the action was carried out and was later referred to at a meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, it's completely unclear what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, the interpreters had a little difficulty understanding. Are you saying they actually staged the events then later they pretended to talk about staging the events, on the 29th and 30th? Is that the explanation that you're offering?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could look at page 6, please. It's actually page 6 in English and in B/C/S. And in B/C/S it is right there at the top of the page, the top paragraph. It says -- the report says: "The decision by our authorities, i.e., the General Staff of the SVK, not to open the motorway served on the Croatian side as the immediate cause and justification before the international community for the aggression against the RSK, i.e., Western Slavonia." And that was the conclusion of this commission; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. We're done with that document. Finally, Mr. Peric, do you agree with me that nothing that you said about what happened in Operation Flash, you talked about crimes said about what happened in Operation Flash, you talked about crimes committed by the Croat side against the Serb side. But you would agree with me, wouldn't you, that none of what you say happened there could have justified crimes, war crimes or crimes against humanity against Croat civilians. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't grasp the gist of your question. Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Of course. I didn't state it very clearly. Let me try a better way. Do you remember telling us about things that happened during Operation Flash, and you've told us how many people you think were killed in the operation. But wouldn't you agree with me that none of that, that you say happened there, none of what you described, could justify subsequent war crimes or crimes against humanity against Croat civilians?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which subsequent war crimes against Croat civilians you're referring to, and I mean in the aftermath of Operation Flash. Which crimes against Croat civilians in the aftermath of Operation Flash are you referring to? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: My question was just more general, actually. Any crimes. What happened in Operation Flash, according to you, that couldn't justify any subsequent crimes against Croat civilians anywhere, could it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're trying to say. I don't understand, that a crime should justify a crime or -- along those lines. This is my understanding, that you're saying that a crime cannot justify a further crime?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Right. That was the point of my question. It was about justification. You agree with me that none of what you said happened in Operation Flash, could justify a crime after that, against Croat civilians?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Isn't that a little bit of an abstract question of law, very abstract, actually?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't necessarily mean it in the legal sense. I want to know his view of it, whether it's about -- simply about justification. That was the point of my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You're asking for his position as a soldier?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. As a JNA, career JNA officer. May the witness answer the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Judge says yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am quite clear about what Mr. Black is imputing, whether what Croatia did during Operation Storm could justify further crimes against Croat civilians, and he's alluding to the shelling of Croatian towns. If that's indeed what Mr. Black is alluding to, then I will tell you the following. Do not follow the logic of some international subjects and say that any fatal loss of a Serb constitutes a crime of lesser gravity. I myself experienced something as a soldier, that a crime committed against a Serb is being suppressed and concealed, and that any other crimes committed against members of other ethnicities are being highlighted. I tell you that there is no graver death or less grave death. All cases of death are equally grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, please don't assume what I'm talking about, and would you please answer the question. You made your speech now. But whatever you say happened in Operation Flash, you agree, don't you, that that doesn't justify war crimes or crimes against humanity, anywhere? Or do you disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree, because you're imputing to me something that is quite abstract.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No, let me --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't understand the base of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not imputing anything to you. I'm asking you a general question. You've said certain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would imagine your question is specific to the issues that happened in Operation Flash? It's not even general.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, that's right, Your Honour. It's specific in the sense that I'm asking about those things that the witness has said happened in Operation Flash, whether those things justify subsequent crimes, if they occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And is that an abstract question?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It's abstract or general in the question. I'm not asking him to say whether it justified a specific crime later or a specific crime in a certain place, but just in general. Can those things that happened be a justification for war crimes or crimes against humanity. That's the gist of my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Are you able to answer the question now? Have I made it more clear to you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In essence, you're referring to an eye for a eye, a tooth for a tooth. So if Croats committed a crime in Varos and in Slovenia, can the Serbs commit a crime against Croats and use the previous crimes committed by Croats as a justification? Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It's close. Why don't you answer that question --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Assume that there were crimes by Croats. Could those crimes -- do those crimes then justify retaliatory crimes by Serbs against civilians?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. In my personal view, war is a very specific stage of affairs. It is difficult to follow one's common sense in that. Taken as a whole, I believe that every crime generates another crime. Therefore, if a crime is committed somewhere and if there is the intention to retaliate, or if you're in a situation where someone has slapped you and you're thinking about whether you want to slap back or offer the other cheek, then I myself would always slap back. That's the gist of my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm not talking about slaps. I'm talking about crimes against humanity and war crimes, the injuring and killing of civilians. That's the context of what I'm putting this question to you. As a JNA officer, were you trained and given some basic familiarity with the laws of war, the rules of war?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. And I hope that I adhered to them to a great extent, unlike my adversaries who did not honour them. Didn't order a single crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting anything about you ordering crimes. I'm asking you a different question. Given this understanding you had about the rules of war, if you thought that crimes had been committed against someone, that didn't justify you in going to kill civilians, did it? That's not a justification for crimes against innocent civilians, is it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which civilians you mean or which crimes, but I know that a crime was committed against Serb civilians in Western Slavonia, and I do have confirmation of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, I submit that this is not a difficult question to understand and you are refusing to answer it. Under your understanding of the laws of war, could -- if you think there are crimes that have been committed, does that justify you in killing innocent civilians or injuring innocent civilians, committing war crimes or crimes against humanity? Are those subsequent crimes justified, in your view? Please just answer that question.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not shrinking from answering your question. I simply don't know what the drift of your question is. I never issued any orders to anyone to open fire upon civilians or to kill civilians by way of retaliation for the massacres committed against the Serb civilians in Western Slavonia. I never ordered something like that to anyone, nor would I.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Especially not against civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir why would you not have done that? I'm not asking about what you did, but you say you would not have ordered crimes against civilians. Why not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not, because a soldier's honour dictates that soldiers should fight against a soldier and not a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Black. I see it is time. Mr. Perovic, will you do your reexamination tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My re-examination will not take longer than 15 or 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, then, we will do it tomorrow because we have come to the end of the day for today. I just wanted to say to you, Mr. Perovic, I just want to invite you to look at Rule 90(H), subrule (i) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence about something that we talked about a little earlier. Court adjourned. We will come again at 9.00 tomorrow morning. Quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon tomorrow. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
